item.title: 1986 5-month-old Andrew De La Pena was running out of time. Only a new heart will save him.
item.description: December 1986. At Stanford, in California, 5-month-old Andrew De La Pena was running out of time. He was born with a rare heart disease. It had taken his older sister the year before. Only a new heart could save him. Then a donor heart was found in Fargo, North Dakota, more than 1,400 miles away. Doctors wanted it transplanted within 4 hours. A Learjet flew a Stanford surgical team up to get it. But that night, in the North Dakota cold, its second engine would not start. A business jet was offered instead. It wasn’t fast enough. With the clock running, North Dakota’s governor called the head of the state’s National Guard. “So we said, ‘Go!’” the general remembered. At the Air Guard base in Fargo, 1st Lt. Bob Becklund was on duty with the F-4 Phantoms. The F-4 has 2 seats and no room for cargo, so his back-seater stayed on the ground. The heart, about the size of a golf ball, rode in the empty back seat in a red and white Playmate cooler. At 3:06 a.m., Becklund took off alone. “That night I was going fast,” he said. Another jet was supposed to meet him in Utah and fly the last leg. It never showed up. “I knew one thing for sure. The heart needed to be in California, not in Utah,” Becklund said. He refueled and was back in the air in 31 minutes. At 4:43 a.m. Pacific time, he landed at Moffett Naval Air Station near San Francisco. A Stanford team was waiting. “I just handed them the Playmate cooler, said ‘thanks, goodnight.’ And that was that.” The transplant was successful. Andrew grew up. He beat cancer as a boy, became a teacher, earned a master’s degree in Amsterdam and learned 5 languages. That’s him in the photo, next to the pilot who flew his heart through the night. “The coolest thing is meeting Andrew,” said Becklund, who later became a general. There was another family in this story. The heart came from Michael McCann, a 4-month-old boy in Fargo who stopped breathing in his sleep. His parents, Karen and Steve, chose to donate it. In 2007, they met Andrew for the first time. Steve said he “just had life in his eyes.”
